q: In a picture there are 3 moons and 6 stars. Which sentence describes the ratio?
img: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 116" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:440px"><text x="24" y="44" font-size="30" fill="#B45309">☾</text><text x="60" y="44" font-size="30" fill="#B45309">☾</text><text x="96" y="44" font-size="30" fill="#B45309">☾</text><text x="24" y="92" font-size="30" fill="#4F46E5">★</text><text x="60" y="92" font-size="30" fill="#4F46E5">★</text><text x="96" y="92" font-size="30" fill="#4F46E5">★</text><text x="132" y="92" font-size="30" fill="#4F46E5">★</text><text x="168" y="92" font-size="30" fill="#4F46E5">★</text><text x="204" y="92" font-size="30" fill="#4F46E5">★</text></svg>
opts: For every 6 moons, there are 3 stars.
For every 9 moons, there are 3 stars.
For every 3 stars, there are 6 moons.
For every 3 moons, there are 6 stars.
why: There are 3 moons and 6 stars, so "for every 3 moons, there are 6 stars." The order of the words must match the order of the numbers.
tip: Read the ratio in the same order as the quantities are named.

q: For every 3 moons there are 6 stars. What is the ratio of moons to stars written with the smallest whole numbers?
why: 3 : 6 — divide both by 3 to get 1 : 2. For every 1 moon there are 2 stars.
tip: Moons come first because the question says "moons to stars."

q: A class has 12 girls and 10 boys. What is the ratio of boys to girls?
why: Boys are named first, so write the number of boys first: 10 : 12.
tip: The first word in "boys to girls" gets the first number.

q: Which is NOT a way to write the ratio "5 cats for every 2 dogs"?
why: 5 : 2, 5 to 2, and the sentence all show cats first. 2 : 5 reverses the order, so it would mean 2 cats for every 5 dogs.
tip: a : b, "a to b" and "for every a there are b" all mean the same ratio.

q: A recipe uses 4 cups of flour and 1 cup of sugar. Which statement is true?
opts: The ratio of sugar to flour is 4 : 1.
The ratio of sugar to flour is 1 : 4.
The ratio of flour to sugar is 1 : 4.
There is 1 cup of flour for every 4 cups of sugar.
why: Sugar is 1 cup and flour is 4 cups, so sugar to flour is 1 : 4 (and flour to sugar is 4 : 1).
tip: Check each statement: which quantity is named first?

q: A fruit bowl has 5 apples, 3 bananas, and 2 pears. What is the ratio of bananas to all the fruit?
why: Total fruit is 5 + 3 + 2 = 10. Bananas to all fruit is 3 : 10.
tip: A ratio can compare a part to the whole, not just part to part.

q: In a survey, 8 students chose pepperoni and 6 chose cheese as their favorite pizza topping. Which statement is correct?
opts: For every 4 students who chose pepperoni, 3 chose cheese.
For every 2 students who chose pepperoni, 1 chose cheese.
For every 4 students who chose cheese, 3 chose pepperoni.
For every 8 students who chose pepperoni, 14 chose cheese.
why: 8 : 6 divides by 2 to give 4 : 3, so for every 4 pepperoni votes there are 3 cheese votes.
tip: Divide both numbers by the same amount to describe the ratio more simply.

q: There are 6 stars and 3 moons. Two more moons are added, but the stars stay the same. What is the new ratio of stars to moons?
why: Moons become 3 + 2 = 5 and stars stay at 6, so the ratio is now 6 : 5. When the numbers change, the ratio changes too.
tip: Recount each quantity after a change before writing the ratio.

q: A bag has red and blue marbles in the ratio 2 : 5. Which could be the actual numbers of marbles?
why: 2 × 4 = 8 and 5 × 4 = 20, so 8 : 20 is the same ratio as 2 : 5. The others do not multiply both parts by the same number.
tip: Actual amounts must be the ratio multiplied by the same number.

q: A rice recipe uses 2 cups of rice for every 3 cups of water. Which is an equivalent ratio of rice to water?
why: Multiply both parts by 2: 2 × 2 = 4 and 3 × 2 = 6, giving 4 : 6.
tip: Equivalent ratios multiply or divide BOTH numbers by the same number.

q: Which ratio is equivalent to 5 : 1?
why: 5 × 3 = 15 and 1 × 3 = 3, so 15 : 3 is equivalent to 5 : 1.
tip: Find what number you multiply the first part by, then do the same to the second.

q: Noah says 3 : 4 and 5 : 6 are equivalent because he added 2 to each number. Is he correct?
opts: No — he should have added 2 to only the first number.
Yes — both ratios have the second number 1 more than the first.
No — equivalent ratios come from multiplying or dividing both numbers by the same number, not adding.
Yes — adding the same number keeps the ratio the same.
why: Adding changes the relationship. 3 : 4 doubled is 6 : 8, not 5 : 6. Only multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number keeps the ratio equivalent.
tip: Test: does one ratio scale to the other by a single multiplier?

q: To make 1 batch of rice, you use 1 cup of rice and 2 cups of water. How much water do you need for 5 batches?
why: 5 batches means multiplying both amounts by 5: 1 × 5 = 5 cups rice and 2 × 5 = 10 cups water.
tip: Each batch is one copy of the ratio — 5 batches is 5 copies.

q: Which pair of ratios is equivalent?
why: Divide 6 : 9 by 3 to get 2 : 3. So 6 : 9 and 2 : 3 are equivalent.
tip: Simplify each ratio and compare.

q: A drink mix uses 3 scoops of powder for every 8 ounces of water. Which mixture will taste the SAME?
why: 3 × 3 = 9 scoops and 8 × 3 = 24 ounces. Same ratio means the same taste.
tip: Same taste means equivalent ratio — check for one common multiplier.

q: Batches of purple paint use 2 cups of blue paint and 3 cups of red paint. If you use 12 cups of red paint, how much blue paint keeps the same color?
why: Red went from 3 to 12, which is × 4. Blue must also be × 4: 2 × 4 = 8 cups.
tip: Find the multiplier on the quantity you know, then use it on the other.

q: Which ratio is NOT equivalent to the others: 4 : 10, 6 : 15, 10 : 25, 8 : 18?
why: 4 : 10, 6 : 15 and 10 : 25 all simplify to 2 : 5. 8 : 18 simplifies to 4 : 9.
tip: Reduce each ratio to simplest form and look for the odd one out.

q: A recipe uses 12 cups of water for 8 cups of rice. Which smaller recipe uses the same ratio?
why: Divide both by 4: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2. So 3 cups water for 2 cups rice.
tip: Dividing both parts by the same number also makes an equivalent ratio.

q: Complete the equivalent ratio: 3 : 7 = 12 : ___
tip: Figure out the multiplier from the parts you know.

q: Complete the equivalent ratio: 45 : 30 = ___ : 2
tip: You can divide to make an equivalent ratio with smaller numbers.

q: A fruit salad uses 4 strawberries for every 6 grapes. Which is NOT an equivalent ratio?
why: 4 : 6 = 2 : 3 = 8 : 12 = 10 : 15. But 6 : 8 is 3 : 4, which is different (it came from adding 2).
tip: Simplify every option to 2 : 3 to test it.

q: Is 7 : 3 equivalent to 21 : 9? Choose the best justification.
opts: No, because 21 and 9 are both odd.
No, because 21 is not a multiple of 9.
why: Both parts of 7 : 3 are multiplied by the same number, 3, to get 21 : 9, so the ratios are equivalent.
tip: Precise justification names the same multiplier for both parts.

q: Lin mixes 5 cups of juice with 2 cups of soda. She wants to make 3 times as much. How many total cups will she have?
why: 3 times as much: 15 cups juice and 6 cups soda. 15 + 6 = 21 cups.
tip: Scale both parts, then add for the total.

q: Which list shows ratios that are all equivalent to 2 : 5?
tip: Each new ratio should be the original times a whole number.

q: The ratio of cats to dogs at a shelter is 3 : 4. There are 24 dogs. How many cats are there?
why: 4 × 6 = 24 dogs, so cats = 3 × 6 = 18.
tip: Find how many "groups" of the ratio there are.

q: Which ratio is equivalent to 18 : 24 AND uses the smallest possible whole numbers?
tip: Divide by the greatest common factor to get the simplest form.

q: A fruit lab drink uses 2 cups of mango and 5 cups of orange juice. Kiran made a drink with the same taste using 35 cups of orange juice. How many cups of mango did he use?
why: 5 × 7 = 35, so mango is 2 × 7 = 14 cups.
tip: Same taste = equivalent ratio. Find the multiplier from 5 to 35.

q: On a double number line for 3 apples costing $2, which pair should line up at the same tick mark?
why: 3 apples : $2. Multiply by 4: 12 apples : $8. Values lined up must be an equivalent ratio.
tip: Pairs at the same tick mark are equivalent ratios.

q: A double number line shows 0, 5, 10, 15 on the top line (liters of water) and 0, 2, 4, 6 on the bottom line (spoons of salt). How much salt goes with 25 liters?
why: Each jump is 5 liters to 2 spoons. 25 liters is 5 jumps, so 5 × 2 = 10 spoons.
tip: Extend the double number line with the same jumps.

q: Which is the same between a ratio table and a double number line that show the same ratio?
opts: Both show pairs of values that are equivalent ratios.
A double number line can only show 3 values.
A table cannot show the value 0.
why: Both representations list equivalent ratios — the table in rows and the number line at lined-up tick marks.
tip: A double number line is like a table turned sideways with evenly spaced values.

q: A double number line for paint uses tick marks 0, 3, 6, 9 for cups of yellow and 0, 4, 8, 12 for cups of blue. Ana says 7 cups of yellow goes with 8 cups of blue because 7 is between 6 and 9. What is her mistake?
opts: She should have added 1 to 8 as well.
7 is not lined up with 8; 6 cups of yellow goes with 8 cups of blue.
Double number lines cannot show yellow paint.
why: Values must be at the SAME tick mark. 8 cups of blue lines up with 6 cups of yellow, not 7.
tip: Read straight up or down the same tick mark.

q: A double number line shows $15 lines up with 6 tickets. How much do 10 tickets cost?
tip: When the multiplier is not a whole number, go to the value for 1 first.

q: 5 tomatoes cost $2.00. What is the price for 1 tomato?
why: $2.00 ÷ 5 = $0.40. A clerk who charges $0.50 for one is overcharging.
tip: Divide the total price by the number of items.

q: A pack of 6 juice boxes costs $3.00. What is the price of 1 juice box?
why: $3.00 ÷ 6 = $0.50 per juice box.
tip: Price for one = total ÷ number of items.

q: Which item has the lowest price for one? A: 2 for $7.00   B: 10 for $24.00   C: 4 for $5.00
why: A: $7 ÷ 2 = $3.50. B: $24 ÷ 10 = $2.40. C: $5 ÷ 4 = $1.25. C is the cheapest per item, even though A has a lower total than B.
tip: Compare price for one, not the total price.

q: 4 bottles of apple juice cost $6.00. How much do 3 bottles cost?
tip: Find the price for one, then multiply.

q: 12 pencils cost $2.40. How much do 8 pencils cost?
tip: Price for one is the bridge between two amounts.

q: 5 notebooks cost $4.00. How much do 10 notebooks cost?
why: 10 is double 5, so double the price: $8.00. (Or $0.80 each × 10.)
tip: Sometimes you can scale the whole ratio without finding the price for one.

q: Naoki is finding the price of 5 cupcakes when 4 cupcakes cost $10. He did $10 ÷ 5 = $2, then $2 × 5 = $10. What should he have done?
opts: Divide $10 by 5 and multiply by 4 to get $8.
Divide $10 by 4 to get $2.50, then multiply by 5 to get $12.50.
why: The price for one is $10 ÷ 4 = $2.50 because $10 buys 4 cupcakes. Then 5 × $2.50 = $12.50.
tip: Divide the price by the number of items it actually buys.

q: Store A sells 3 bananas for $1. Store B sells 8 bananas for $2. Which is the better deal and why?
opts: Store A, because 3 bananas is fewer to carry.
Store A, because $1 is less than $2.
Store B, because each banana costs $0.25 instead of about $0.33.
why: A: $1 ÷ 3 ≈ $0.33 each. B: $2 ÷ 8 = $0.25 each. Store B is cheaper per banana.
tip: A better deal means a lower price for one.

q: 6 muffins cost $9.00. Maria has $20. What is the greatest number of muffins she can buy?
tip: Round down when you can only buy whole items.

q: What is the least common multiple of 4 and 6?
why: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12… Multiples of 6: 6, 12… The first one they share is 12.
tip: List multiples of each number until you find the first match.

q: Which list shows the first three common multiples of 3 and 5?
why: Common multiples of 3 and 5 are multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45.
tip: Common multiples are numbers in BOTH skip-counting lists.

q: What is the LCM of 8 and 12?
why: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. Multiples of 12: 12, 24. The LCM is 24.
tip: The product (96) is a common multiple, but not always the least.

q: What is the LCM of 7 and 5?
why: 7 and 5 share no factors except 1, so their LCM is 7 × 5 = 35.
tip: When two numbers share no factors, the LCM is their product.

q: Hot dogs come in packs of 10 and buns come in packs of 8. What is the fewest of each you can buy to have the same number of hot dogs and buns?
why: The LCM of 10 and 8 is 40. That means 4 packs of hot dogs and 5 packs of buns.
tip: "The fewest to match up" is an LCM problem.

q: One light blinks every 6 seconds and another every 9 seconds. They blink together now. In how many seconds will they next blink together?
why: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18. Multiples of 9: 9, 18. They meet at 18 seconds.
tip: Events that repeat on different schedules line up at the LCM.

q: What is the LCM of 12 and 18?
why: Multiples of 18: 18, 36. 36 is also a multiple of 12 (12 × 3). So the LCM is 36.
tip: Skip-count by the larger number and check each against the smaller.

q: Which pair of numbers has an LCM of 20?
why: Multiples of 10: 10, 20. 20 is also a multiple of 4, and 10 is not, so LCM(4, 10) = 20. LCM(2, 10) = 10, LCM(3, 10) = 30 and LCM(6, 10) = 30.
tip: Test each pair by listing multiples of the larger number.

q: Bus A leaves every 15 minutes and Bus B every 20 minutes. Both leave at 8:00 a.m. When do they next leave together?
why: LCM of 15 and 20: 15, 30, 45, 60 — and 60 is a multiple of 20. 60 minutes after 8:00 is 9:00 a.m.
tip: Find the LCM in minutes, then add it to the start time.

q: What is the greatest common factor of 12 and 18?
why: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The greatest shared factor is 6.
tip: List all factors of both numbers and pick the largest one in both lists.

q: Which number is a common factor of 20 and 30?
why: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 and 30 ÷ 5 = 6, so 5 divides both.
tip: A common factor divides both numbers with no remainder.

q: What is the GCF of 16 and 40?
why: Factors of 16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. 40 ÷ 8 = 5 but 40 ÷ 16 is not whole, so the GCF is 8.
tip: Start with the smaller number’s largest factors and test them.

q: What is the GCF of 9 and 14?
why: 9 has factors 1, 3, 9. 14 has factors 1, 2, 7, 14. The only shared factor is 1.
tip: If two numbers share nothing but 1, the GCF is 1.

q: A teacher has 24 pencils and 36 erasers. She wants identical kits with no supplies left over. What is the greatest number of kits she can make?
why: GCF(24, 36) = 12. Each kit gets 2 pencils and 3 erasers.
tip: "Split into equal groups, as many as possible" is a GCF problem.

q: Which situation is solved using the LCM instead of the GCF?
opts: Finding when two runners on different lap times will next be at the start together.
Cutting two ribbons into the longest equal pieces with nothing left over.
Packing 30 apples and 45 oranges into identical bags.
Splitting 18 boys and 24 girls into the most equal teams.
why: Lining up repeating events (laps) uses common multiples. The other three split things into equal groups, which uses common factors.
tip: Splitting into groups → GCF. Repeating until things match → LCM.

q: Use the GCF to write 36 + 48 as a product: ___ × (3 + 4).
tip: Factor out the GCF using the distributive property.

q: A rectangle that is 18 cm by 30 cm is covered exactly by the largest possible square tiles. What is the side length of each tile?
why: The side must divide both 18 and 30. The greatest such number is GCF(18, 30) = 6 cm.
tip: The largest square tile that fits evenly uses the GCF of the side lengths.

q: Juice comes in packs of 12 and snacks in packs of 8. (a) What is the fewest of each to buy so the amounts match, and (b) into how many identical bags could 12 juices and 8 snacks be split with nothing left over (as many bags as possible)?
why: (a) Matching amounts uses LCM(12, 8) = 24. (b) Equal groups use GCF(12, 8) = 4, so 4 bags with 3 juices and 2 snacks each.
tip: Decide for each part: matching totals (LCM) or splitting (GCF)?

q: Paint A uses 2 cups blue to 3 cups red. Paint B uses 4 cups blue to 6 cups red. How do the colors compare?
why: 4 : 6 is 2 : 3 multiplied by 2, so the ratios are equivalent and the colors are the same.
tip: Equivalent ratios make the same color.

q: Recipe A: 3 cups blue and 5 cups yellow. Recipe B: 3 cups blue and 4 cups yellow. Which green is more yellow?
why: Both use 3 cups of blue, so compare the yellow: 5 > 4. Recipe A is more yellow.
tip: When one quantity is the same, just compare the other.

q: Purple paint is made with 2 tsp blue and 3 tsp red. Han uses 3 tsp blue and 2 tsp red. Is his purple the same color?
opts: No — he has more blue than red, but the recipe has more red than blue.
No — he needs 5 tsp of blue.
why: The recipe is blue : red = 2 : 3. Han’s is 3 : 2. Same total does not mean same ratio, so it is a different color.
tip: The order of the quantities matters.

q: Lemonade A uses 2 scoops mix in 5 cups water. Lemonade B uses 3 scoops mix in 6 cups water. Which is stronger?
why: Make the water the same: A is 12 : 30 and B is 15 : 30. B has more mix in the same water, so it is stronger.
tip: Scale both ratios so one quantity matches, then compare the other.

q: Class A has 4 teachers for 60 students. Class B has 3 teachers for 48 students. Which class has more students per teacher?
why: A: 60 ÷ 4 = 15 students per teacher. B: 48 ÷ 3 = 16 students per teacher. B has more.
tip: Compare by finding the amount for 1.

q: Orange paint: Mix A is 6 cups red to 4 cups yellow. Mix B is 9 cups red to 6 cups yellow. Mix C is 8 cups red to 6 cups yellow. Which mix is a different shade?
why: A = 3 : 2 and B = 3 : 2 (both simplify). C = 4 : 3, which is different.
tip: Simplify each ratio to compare all of them at once.

q: Diego runs 5 laps in 8 minutes. Noah runs 7 laps in 12 minutes. Who runs faster?
opts: They run at the same speed
why: Make the minutes match at 24: Diego 15 laps, Noah 14 laps. Diego runs more laps in the same time.
tip: Use a common value (like the LCM of the minutes) to compare.

q: Trail mix A has 3 cups nuts to 2 cups raisins. Trail mix B has 5 cups nuts to 4 cups raisins. Which mix has the greater ratio of nuts to raisins?
why: Match raisins at 4: A becomes 6 : 4 and B is 5 : 4. A has more nuts for the same raisins.
tip: Pick the quantity that is easiest to make equal.

q: Which drink has the most juice compared to water? A: 2 juice : 3 water   B: 3 juice : 4 water   C: 5 juice : 8 water
why: Juice per 1 cup of water: A = 2 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.67, B = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75, C = 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625. B is the most juicy.
tip: With three ratios, compare the amount per 1 of the same quantity.

tip: Each row in a ratio table is the first row times the same number.

q: A city stocks 2 power strips for every 25 people. How many power strips are needed for 200 people?
why: 200 ÷ 25 = 8, so multiply both by 8: 2 × 8 = 16 power strips.
tip: Choose a multiplier that jumps straight to the large number.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 2.9 (Ratio Tables with Large Quantities)
q: A recommendation is 3 handheld showers for every 50 people. How many showers for 1,000 people?
tip: Multiplying by 10 or 100 is a fast way through big numbers.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 2.9 (Ratio Tables with Large Quantities)
q: Use the table. What is the missing value?
img: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 148" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:300px"><rect x="20" y="10" width="130" height="32" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85.0" y="31" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">Cups of mix</text><rect x="150" y="10" width="130" height="32" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="215.0" y="31" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">Servings</text><rect x="20" y="42" width="130" height="32" fill="#fff" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85.0" y="63" font-size="14" font-weight="400" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">5</text><rect x="150" y="42" width="130" height="32" fill="#fff" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="215.0" y="63" font-size="14" font-weight="400" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">40</text><rect x="20" y="74" width="130" height="32" fill="#fff" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85.0" y="95" font-size="14" font-weight="400" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">10</text><rect x="150" y="74" width="130" height="32" fill="#fff" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="215.0" y="95" font-size="14" font-weight="400" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">80</text><rect x="20" y="106" width="130" height="32" fill="#fff" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85.0" y="127" font-size="14" font-weight="400" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">15</text><rect x="150" y="106" width="130" height="32" fill="#fff" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="215.0" y="127" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#4F46E5" text-anchor="middle">?</text></svg>
why: 5 cups makes 40 servings → 8 servings per cup. 15 cups × 8 = 120 servings.
tip: Look for a row you can scale easily to the row you need.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 2.9 (Ratio Tables with Large Quantities)
q: A school orders 4 air pumps for every 120 students. How many air pumps does it need for 900 students?
why: 4 pumps : 120 students = 1 pump : 30 students. 900 ÷ 30 = 30 pumps.
tip: Divide down to a friendly row, then multiply up.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 2.9 (Ratio Tables with Large Quantities)
q: In a ratio table, 6 tickets cost $42. Which row also belongs in the table?
why: Multiply both by 10: 60 tickets cost $420. Adding 1 or 6 to each value does not keep the ratio.
tip: Rows must be multiples of each other.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 2.9 (Ratio Tables with Large Quantities)
q: A factory makes 360 toys every 8 hours. At that rate, how many toys does it make in 50 hours?
why: 360 ÷ 8 = 45 toys per hour. 45 × 50 = 2,250 toys.
tip: Find the value for 1, then scale to the large number.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 2.9 (Ratio Tables with Large Quantities)
q: A food bank packs 7 cans for every 2 families. How many cans for 150 families?
tip: Use the multiplier 150 ÷ 2.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 2.9 (Ratio Tables with Large Quantities)
q: A shelter needs 9 blankets for every 12 people. How many people can be served with 300 blankets?
why: 9 : 12 simplifies to 3 : 4. 300 ÷ 3 = 100, so people = 4 × 100 = 400.
tip: Simplify the ratio first to make big-number scaling easier.

q: It takes 4 balloons to decorate 1 table. How many tables can be decorated with 36 balloons?
why: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 tables.
tip: Divide when you know the total and the amount per group.

q: A balloon pump fills 3 balloons in 2 minutes. How many balloons does it fill in 10 minutes?
why: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, so multiply both by 5: 3 × 5 = 15 balloons.
tip: Find the multiplier from the minutes.

q: 6 bags of balloons cost $15. How much do 10 bags cost?
tip: When the multiplier is not whole, go through the value for 1.

q: A car travels 150 miles on 5 gallons of gas. How far can it go on 8 gallons?
why: 150 ÷ 5 = 30 miles per gallon. 30 × 8 = 240 miles.
tip: Divide down to 1, multiply up to what you need.

q: Which strategy correctly finds the cost of 15 pens if 6 pens cost $9?
opts: Subtract 6 from 15 and add that many dollars.
Divide 6 and $9 by 3 to get 2 pens for $3, then multiply by 7.5 — or find $1.50 each and multiply by 15.
why: Both correct strategies give $22.50: $9 ÷ 6 = $1.50 each, and $1.50 × 15 = $22.50.
tip: Any strategy works if you multiply or divide both quantities by the same number.

q: A recipe needs 4 eggs for 10 pancakes. How many eggs are needed for 25 pancakes?
why: 4 eggs : 10 pancakes = 2 eggs : 5 pancakes. 25 is 5 × 5, so 2 × 5 = 10 eggs.
tip: Divide to a smaller equivalent ratio that reaches the target evenly.

q: A party store sells 8 balloons for $6. Mrs. Lee needs 60 balloons. How much will they cost?
tip: Price per balloon makes any amount easy to find.

q: A printer prints 45 pages in 3 minutes. How long does it take to print 270 pages?
why: 45 ÷ 3 = 15 pages per minute. 270 ÷ 15 = 18 minutes.
tip: Find the unit rate, then divide the total by it.

q: A machine fills 12 balloons in 5 minutes. A second machine fills 20 balloons in 8 minutes. Together, how many balloons do they fill in 40 minutes?
tip: Solve for each machine separately, then combine.

q: Green paint uses blue and yellow in the ratio 2 : 3. How many cups of blue are in 10 cups of green paint?
img: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:440px"><text x="8" y="37" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#2B3242">Blue</text><rect x="90" y="15" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="134" y="15" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><text x="8" y="87" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#2B3242">Yellow</text><rect x="90" y="65" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="134" y="65" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="178" y="65" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/></svg>
why: The tape diagram has 2 + 3 = 5 equal parts. 10 ÷ 5 = 2 cups per part. Blue = 2 parts × 2 = 4 cups.
tip: Add the parts to find the total number of boxes.

q: Purple paint uses 2 tsp blue for every 3 tsp red. How much purple paint does one batch make?
why: One batch is 2 + 3 = 5 tsp of purple paint.
tip: The whole is the sum of the parts.

q: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is 3 : 5. There are 40 students in all. How many are girls?
why: 3 + 5 = 8 parts. 40 ÷ 8 = 5 students per part. Girls = 5 × 5 = 25.
tip: Total ÷ number of parts = size of one part.

q: Purple paint is 2 parts blue to 3 parts red. You need 15 tsp of purple paint. How many tsp of red?
why: 5 parts make 15 tsp, so 1 part = 3 tsp. Red = 3 × 3 = 9 tsp.
tip: Start with the total when you know the whole.

q: Each box of the tape diagram has the same value. If the total is 56, what is the value of one box?
img: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:440px"><text x="8" y="37" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#2B3242">Cats</text><rect x="90" y="15" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="134" y="15" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="178" y="15" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><text x="8" y="87" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#2B3242">Dogs</text><rect x="90" y="65" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="134" y="65" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="178" y="65" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="222" y="65" width="44" height="34" fill="#EEF1F8" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="2"/></svg>
why: There are 3 + 4 = 7 boxes in all. 56 ÷ 7 = 8 per box.
tip: Count every box in both rows.

q: A trail mix uses peanuts to raisins in a 5 : 2 ratio. There are 9 more cups of peanuts than raisins. How many cups of trail mix are there?
why: The difference is 5 − 2 = 3 parts = 9 cups, so 1 part = 3 cups. Total = 7 parts × 3 = 21 cups (15 peanuts, 6 raisins).
tip: The difference between parts is also a number of boxes.

q: Orange juice and soda are mixed in a 4 : 1 ratio. Jada makes 3 cups of punch using 2.4 cups of juice. Is her punch the same recipe?
opts: Yes — 4 : 1 means juice is 4 out of 5 parts, and 4/5 of 3 cups is 2.4 cups.
No — she needs 4 cups of juice.
Yes — any punch with juice and soda is the same.
No — there should be 3 cups of soda.
why: 5 parts = 3 cups, so 1 part = 0.6 cup. Juice = 4 × 0.6 = 2.4 cups and soda = 0.6 cup. It matches.
tip: Check: total ÷ total parts, then multiply by the part you want.

q: A hospital has nurses and patients in a ratio of 1 : 4. There are 80 people in all. How many nurses are there?
why: 1 + 4 = 5 parts. 80 ÷ 5 = 16, so there are 16 nurses and 64 patients.
tip: Use the total number of parts to share out the whole.

q: A bag has red, blue and green tiles in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. There are 18 blue tiles. How many tiles in all?
why: Blue is 3 parts = 18, so 1 part = 6. Total = (2 + 3 + 5) × 6 = 10 × 6 = 60 tiles.
tip: Use the part you know to find one box, then count all boxes.

q: Adult and student tickets are sold in a ratio of 3 : 10. A total of 78 tickets were sold. How many were adult tickets?
why: 3 + 10 = 13 parts. 78 ÷ 13 = 6 per part. Adults = 3 × 6 = 18 and students = 60.
tip: Divide the total by the sum of the ratio parts.

q: A city plan uses land for parks and buildings in the ratio 2 : 7. The city has 90 acres. How many acres are parks?
why: 2 + 7 = 9 parts. 90 ÷ 9 = 10 acres per part. Parks = 2 × 10 = 20 acres.
tip: Draw a tape diagram with 9 equal boxes.

q: The ratio of fiction to non-fiction books on a shelf is 5 : 3. There are 15 non-fiction books. How many books are there in all?
why: Non-fiction is 3 parts = 15, so 1 part = 5. Total = 8 parts × 5 = 40 books.
tip: When you know a part, start with the part — not the total.

q: Bard paid $26 for 4 tickets, Andre paid $29 for 4 tickets, and Mai paid $31.25 for 5 tickets. Who paid the lowest price per ticket?
why: Bard: $26 ÷ 4 = $6.50. Andre: $29 ÷ 4 = $7.25. Mai: $31.25 ÷ 5 = $6.25. Mai paid the least per ticket.
tip: Divide the total price by the number of tickets.

q: A town has houses and apartments in the ratio 4 : 5. There are 30 more apartments than houses. How many homes are there in all?
why: The difference is 5 − 4 = 1 part = 30. Total = 9 parts × 30 = 270 homes.
tip: The difference in parts tells you the value of one part.

q: Blue and yellow paint make green paint in a 1 : 3 ratio. Lin wants 20 cups of green paint but has only 4 cups of blue. Does she have enough?
opts: No — she needs 5 cups of blue.
Yes — she needs only 4 cups of blue.
Yes — she needs only 1 cup of blue.
No — she needs 15 cups of blue.
why: 1 + 3 = 4 parts. 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cups per part. Blue is 1 part = 5 cups, so 4 cups is not enough.
tip: Find the size of one part from the whole first.

q: A school garden has tomatoes, peppers and beans planted in a 3 : 2 : 1 ratio. There are 72 plants. How many more tomato plants than bean plants are there?
why: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 parts; 72 ÷ 6 = 12 per part. Tomatoes = 36, beans = 12. 36 − 12 = 24.
tip: Find each part, then answer the exact question asked.

q: A soccer team won 3 games for every 2 games it lost (no ties). It played 35 games. How many more games did it win than lose?
why: 3 + 2 = 5 parts; 35 ÷ 5 = 7 per part. Wins = 21, losses = 14. 21 − 14 = 7.
tip: The difference is 1 part, so it equals one box.

q: Same recipe? A purple paint recipe is 2 tsp blue : 3 tsp red. Kiran made 5 tsp of purple with 3 tsp of blue. Choose the best explanation.
opts: Same — he only swapped the numbers.
Not the same — 5 tsp of purple should use 2 tsp blue and 3 tsp red.
Not the same — 5 tsp of purple needs 5 tsp of blue.
why: One batch of the recipe is exactly 5 tsp: 2 blue + 3 red. Using 3 blue changes the ratio to 3 : 2, a different color.
tip: Use a table of the recipe to check the parts for the total you have.

q: How many inches are in 4 feet? (1 foot = 12 inches)
why: 1 ft : 12 in, so 4 ft : 48 in.
tip: Converting to a smaller unit gives a bigger number.

q: How many feet are in 15 yards? (1 yard = 3 feet)
why: 1 yd : 3 ft. Multiply by 15: 15 yd : 45 ft.
tip: Use the ratio 1 yd : 3 ft as a ratio table.

q: How many yards are in 15 feet?
why: 3 ft : 1 yd. 15 ÷ 3 = 5 yards.
tip: Converting to a larger unit gives a smaller number.

q: Marco wants to convert 15 feet to yards. He set up the table with 3 ft over 1 yd, and wrote 15 under the 1 yd. What did he do wrong?
opts: He should have used 12 instead of 3.
15 is feet, so it belongs in the same column as the 3 ft.
why: In a ratio table, each column must hold the same unit. 15 feet goes under 3 feet, giving 15 ft : 5 yd.
tip: Keep like units lined up together.

q: A flagpole is 14 yards tall. How many feet tall is it?
why: 1 yd = 3 ft, so 14 × 3 = 42 feet.
tip: Multiply when going from a larger unit to a smaller one.

q: How many ounces are in 3.5 pounds? (1 pound = 16 ounces)
tip: Multiply by the number of small units in one large unit.

q: Jada converted 8 feet to inches by doing 8 × 12. Han did 12 × 8. Who is correct?
opts: Both — they both found 96 inches; the order of multiplying does not matter.
why: Both use the ratio 1 ft : 12 in. 8 × 12 = 12 × 8 = 96 inches.
tip: Multiplication is commutative, so either order works.

q: A water jug holds 3 gallons. How many quarts is that? (1 gallon = 4 quarts)
why: 1 gal : 4 qt, so 3 gal : 12 qt.
tip: Write the conversion as a ratio and scale it.

q: A ribbon is 2.5 meters long. How many centimeters long is it? (1 m = 100 cm)
tip: Metric conversions multiply or divide by powers of 10.

q: A recipe needs 3 cups of milk. A cup is 8 fluid ounces, and Elena has a 20-fluid-ounce bottle. Does she have enough?
why: 3 cups × 8 fl oz = 24 fl oz. 20 fl oz is 4 fluid ounces short.
tip: Convert to the same unit before comparing.

q: A sixth grader walks 10 meters in 8 seconds. What is the walking speed in meters per second?
why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 10 ÷ 8 = 1.25 meters per second.
tip: Speed is a unit rate: distance for 1 unit of time.

q: At 10 meters in 8 seconds, how long does it take to walk 5 meters?
why: 5 meters is half of 10 meters, so it takes half of 8 seconds: 4 seconds.
tip: Half the distance takes half the time at the same speed.

q: At 10 meters in 8 seconds, how long does it take to walk 18 meters?
why: 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8 seconds per meter. 18 × 0.8 = 14.4 seconds.
tip: You can use seconds per meter to find the time for any distance.

q: A cheetah runs 100 meters in 4 seconds. What is its speed?
why: 100 ÷ 4 = 25 meters per second.
tip: Divide distance by time.

q: Runner A runs 200 meters in 25 seconds. Runner B runs 150 meters in 20 seconds. Who is faster?
why: A: 200 ÷ 25 = 8 m/s. B: 150 ÷ 20 = 7.5 m/s. A covers more meters each second.
tip: To compare speeds, find meters per second for each.

q: Two people run the same 400-meter track. One takes 80 seconds and the other takes 100 seconds. Which statement is true?
opts: The 80-second runner is faster, at 4 m/s versus 5 m/s.
They are the same speed because they ran the same distance.
The 80-second runner is faster, at 5 m/s versus 4 m/s.
why: 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m/s and 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m/s. Less time for the same distance means faster.
tip: Same distance? The shorter time is faster.

q: A world-record swimmer swims 50 meters in 20 seconds. At that speed, how far would the swimmer go in 1 minute?
why: 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 m/s. 1 minute = 60 seconds. 2.5 × 60 = 150 meters.
tip: Convert minutes to seconds before using a meters-per-second rate.

q: A train travels 300 km in 4 hours. A car travels 210 km in 3 hours. Which is faster, and by how much?
opts: The car, by 5 km per hour
The train, by 5 km per hour
The train, by 90 km per hour
tip: Find each unit rate, then subtract.

q: A snail moves 3 meters in 4 minutes. How many minutes will it take to move 15 meters?
why: 15 ÷ 3 = 5 groups of 3 meters. 5 × 4 = 20 minutes.
tip: Scale the time by the same factor as the distance.

q: Model train A travels 30 inches in 5 seconds. Train B travels 50 inches in 10 seconds. Which is faster?
why: A: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 in/s. B: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 in/s. A is faster.
tip: Compare inches per second.

q: Store 1 sells 3 pounds of apples for $4.50. Store 2 sells 5 pounds for $7. Which is the better buy?
why: Store 1: $4.50 ÷ 3 = $1.50/lb. Store 2: $7 ÷ 5 = $1.40/lb. Store 2 is cheaper per pound.
tip: Compare price per pound.

q: Which is the faster typing rate: 120 words in 3 minutes or 210 words in 5 minutes?
tip: Find words per minute for both.

q: A model train goes 2 feet per second. Another goes 30 inches per second. Which is faster? (1 foot = 12 inches)
why: 2 ft/s = 24 in/s. 30 in/s > 24 in/s, so the second train is faster.
tip: Convert to the same units before comparing rates.

q: Elena runs 1 mile in 10 minutes. Kiran runs 2,000 meters in 12 minutes. About 1 mile is 1,600 meters. Who is faster?
why: Elena: 1,600 ÷ 10 = 160 meters per minute. Kiran: 2,000 ÷ 12 ≈ 167 meters per minute. Kiran is faster.
tip: Make the units match, then find the rate per minute.

q: Water fills Tank A at 18 liters every 3 minutes and Tank B at 50 liters every 10 minutes. How much more water does Tank A get in 1 hour?
why: A: 6 L/min × 60 = 360 L. B: 5 L/min × 60 = 300 L. Difference = 60 L.
tip: Use unit rates to compare over any time.

q: Train X travels 45 meters in 15 seconds. Train Y travels 200 meters in 1 minute. Which train is faster?
tip: Change minutes to seconds so both rates use the same units.

q: Package A: 16 oz of cereal for $4.00. Package B: 2 pounds of cereal for $7.20. Which costs less per ounce? (1 lb = 16 oz)
tip: Convert pounds to ounces first.

q: Soft serve costs $6 for 3 cups. What is the price per cup?
why: $6 ÷ 3 = $2 per cup.
tip: "Per" means "for each one".

q: Soft serve costs $6 for 3 cups. How many cups can you buy per dollar?
why: 3 cups ÷ $6 = 0.5 cup per dollar.
tip: Every ratio has two unit rates: a ÷ b and b ÷ a.

q: A ratio is 4 cups of flour to 5 cakes. What are its two unit rates?
opts: 4 cups per cake and 5 cakes per cup
0.8 cup per cake and 0.8 cake per cup
0.8 cup per cake and 1.25 cakes per cup
9 cups per cake and 1 cake per cup
why: 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 cup per cake. 5 ÷ 4 = 1.25 cakes per cup.
tip: Divide each quantity by the other to get the two unit rates.

q: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 2 cups of rice. Which unit rate tells how much water for 1 cup of rice?
opts: 1.5 cups of water per cup of rice
5 cups of water per cup of rice
6 cups of water per cup of rice
0.67 cup of water per cup of rice
why: Water ÷ rice = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 cups of water per cup of rice.
tip: Put the "per" quantity in the divisor.

q: 12 ounces of frozen yogurt cost $3. Which pair of unit rates is correct?
opts: $0.25 per ounce and 0.25 ounce per dollar
$36 per ounce and 15 ounces per dollar
$0.25 per ounce and 4 ounces per dollar
$4 per ounce and 0.25 ounce per dollar
why: $3 ÷ 12 = $0.25 per ounce. 12 ÷ $3 = 4 ounces per dollar.
tip: The two unit rates are reciprocals of each other.

q: It takes 20 minutes to paint 5 boards. Which unit rate is most useful to find how many boards are painted in 2 hours?
opts: 0.25 board per minute, so 30 boards in 120 minutes
20 boards, because 2 hours is 20 minutes × 6 and 5 − 1 = 4
why: 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25 board per minute. 2 hours = 120 minutes. 120 × 0.25 = 30 boards. (Or 120 ÷ 4 minutes per board = 30.)
tip: Choose the unit rate that has the unknown quantity "per" the known one.

q: A soft-serve machine makes 15 cups in 6 minutes. How many minutes per cup?
why: 6 minutes ÷ 15 cups = 0.4 minute per cup (and 2.5 cups per minute).
tip: Minutes per cup = minutes ÷ cups.

q: Lin bought 5 pounds of grapes for $8. She wants to know how many pounds she can get for $20. Which calculation works?
why: Pounds per dollar = 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625. 0.625 × 20 = 12.5 pounds.
tip: Pick the unit rate that is "what you want per what you have".

q: A car uses 1 gallon of gas every 32 miles. How many gallons does it need for 192 miles?
why: 192 ÷ 32 = 6 gallons.
tip: Divide the total by the unit rate.

q: A worker earns $15 per hour. How much does the worker earn in 7.5 hours?
tip: Multiply the unit rate by the number of units.

q: A faucet drips 3 liters every 12 minutes. How many liters does it drip in 1 hour?
why: 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25 liter per minute. 0.25 × 60 = 15 liters.
tip: Change the hour into minutes so the units match.

q: Which is the best buy for juice?
why: Compare the price per ounce: $0.07 is the lowest, so the 64-oz bottle is the best buy.
tip: The best buy has the lowest unit price.

q: A printer prints 18 pages per minute. How long will it take to print 270 pages?
why: 270 ÷ 18 = 15 minutes.
tip: Total ÷ rate = time.

q: Diego’s heart beats 72 times per minute. How many times does it beat in 15 seconds?
why: 15 seconds is 1/4 of a minute. 72 ÷ 4 = 18 beats.
tip: Find what fraction of the unit you need.

q: Paint covers 350 square feet per gallon. A wall is 1,225 square feet. Paint only comes in whole gallons. How many gallons must be bought?
why: 1,225 ÷ 350 = 3.5 gallons, so 4 whole gallons are needed.
tip: Round up when you need enough to finish the job.

q: Bike A goes 36 km in 2 hours. Bike B goes 50 km in 2.5 hours. How much farther does Bike B go than Bike A in 5 hours?
tip: Find both unit rates, then use them for the same time.
